html:
Thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried around 210 BCE beside the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of China, near modern Xi'an. They were meant to guard him in the afterlife.

Farmers digging a well in 1974 found the first pieces. Three main pits hold, by estimates from 2007, more than 8,000 soldiers, about 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses. Most are still in the ground. Each figure was built from moulded parts and then finished by hand, so faces, hair and armour differ. Height follows rank, with generals the tallest. The figures were once painted in bright colours and carried real bronze weapons.

Later digs found other pits with officials, acrobats, strongmen and musicians, which suggests the tomb copied a whole court, not just an army.

The army shows what the new Qin state could do. Only a government that could count, organise and feed huge workforces could make so many figures to one standard. The same state built roads and canals and joined frontier walls into the Great Wall. The emperor's own burial mound nearby has never been opened.
sum: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried around 210 BCE beside the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of China, near modern Xi'an. They were meant to guard him in the afterlife.
